references.text: The context for the parable of the great banquet, where a man invites many guests, but they begin to make excuses — [ref:Luk 14:15-17|Luke 14:15-17].
In Matthew's parallel parable about the king's wedding feast, the invited guests similarly decline the invitation and go off to their own affairs — [ref:Matt 22:2-6|Matthew 22:2-6].
Jesus' words that no one can serve two masters. The excuses of the invited show how earthly possessions compete with God's kingdom — [ref:Matt 6:24|Matthew 6:24].

Paul warns against greed for wealth that leads people away from the faith, just as the first guest's purchase of a field became more important than the invitation — [ref:1 Tim 6:9-10|1 Timothy 6:9-10].
Warning against rejecting the one who speaks; parallel to how the invited reject the host's invitation — [ref:Heb 12:25|Hebrews 12:25].
Wisdom calls out, but people refuse to listen and turn away from its advice—an Old Testament picture of what happens in the parable — [ref:Ordsp 1:24-25|Proverbs 1:24-25].
Other examples of people who want to follow Jesus but first want to settle earthly matters—excuses similar to those in the banquet parable — [ref:Luk 9:59-62|Luke 9:59-62].
Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles because the Jews rejected God's word—a fulfillment of the parable's message that the originally invited would not come — [ref:Apg 13:46|Acts 13:46].
Lot tried to warn his sons-in-law, but they did not take it seriously—an early example of serious invitations being rejected — [ref:1 Mos 19:14|Genesis 19:14].
